note: Receiver labels are reused across hardware changes: reports and corpus entries before and after a swap both say 'lnb-c'. These boundaries are the only way to separate them. Split on capture start time, not on label. A boundary can move a receiver on a radio nobody touched: pluto-5d4d.lnb-a jumped +566 kHz across the pluto-19f2 swap window, which was recorded here as leaving 5d4d valid. Split on capture start time for every radio, not only the one that was worked on. Absolute per-receiver centres for every epoch were measured in section 16 of the detector-evaluation report and are recorded here; a differential alone leaves both ports of a radio free to sit 150 kHz off together, which is what lnb-b and lnb-d do.

lnb-c.reconciliation: section 16a measures +420,686 Hz, spread [+402,447, +438,925]. The +430,700 recorded here sits inside that bracket; both stand.

lnb-d.reconciliation: section 16a measures +14,996 Hz, spread [+12,280, +17,712], n=14,602. The +20,000 recorded here is OUTSIDE that bracket. It came from a 13-point lo_sweep with SE 5,800; the section 16 value draws on two independent populations and supersedes it. Kept as recorded rather than overwritten, because the lo_sweep is what the epoch was declared from.

measured.survey_active_basis: 351 probes / 2808 tunings per receiver over 23.5 h before the swap

epochs.fault: lnb-c detected 3.3x less often than lnb-d. Its +430 kHz LO offset costs only ~10% of survey score (the survey spans +/-700 kHz centred on zero and does not use receiver_centers), so the offset does not explain the deficit. The unit had a separate hardware fault.

epochs.hardware_note: Both units replaced at once and are identical to each other. Identical model does not imply identical LO: free-running crystals, no shared 10 MHz reference in the chain, so the two offsets are independent draws. Measured, both ports are +43.6 and -14.7 ppm at a 9.75 GHz LO: independent draws, as predicted, and both inside an ordinary LNB specification.

epochs.fault: lnb-a's LO moved about +566 kHz across the same window that brackets pluto-19f2's LNB swap, even though 5d4d was believed untouched. Its fire rate stepped 8.26% -> 0.24% while lnb-b was unchanged at 6.49% -> 6.87%, and its surviving detections pinned at +349.8 kHz, the search-grid edge. This single event produced BOTH the 'flat ~1.19 peak-to-median, dead port' exclusion in cross_radio.DEAD_RECEIVERS AND the stale receiver_centers_hz. They are one fault, not two: the port was never dead, it moved out of the search.
epochs.why_it_cannot_self_heal: acquisition.py builds frequency_offsets = arange(-350_000, 350_001, 25_000) + centre, where centre is the ALREADY APPLIED receiver_centers value. A port anchored near zero is blind past about +/-356 kHz and can never discover that it has moved. pluto-19f2's replacement LNB was findable only because its stale +434 kHz calibration had already displaced its grid into range. The daily timer will keep returning ~0 Hz for this port forever; the value must be written as measured_centers_hz from the survey path.
epochs.action: set measured_centers_hz: [396959.5, -170442.5] for pluto-5d4d. SUPERSEDES the earlier [567402.0, 0.0]: that pair carried the differential into rx0 and anchored rx1 at zero, which is right for lnb-a and leaves lnb-b sitting 149 kHz off, costing about a quarter of its detections for no reason. Measuring both ports absolutely is what made the difference visible.
